How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

While impartiality is often regarded as a moral virtue, acting impartially can violate social expectations and relational obligations, creating tension between competing moral considerations. The present research (N = 3,417) examined how people evaluate partial and impartial actors who prioritized either a socially connected other (family member, friend, or community member) or a stranger in need. Across sacrificial dilemmas and more ecologically valid helping scenarios, partial actors were judged more moral and trustworthy than impartial actors. This preference was strongest when impartial actors failed to prioritize a close (family member or friend), rather than more distant (community member), social tie. Impartial actors were also perceived as less predictable and as fulfilling less of their relational obligations, with these perceptions predicting judgments of their moral character. In Experiment 4, participants themselves exhibited a preference for partiality, with most preferring to help a socially connected other over a stranger in greater need. This preference was stronger when decisions were described as publicly observable rather than anonymous, consistent with reputational concerns influencing helping decisions. Together, these findings suggest that everyday moral judgments reflect not only assessments of adherence to abstract ethical principles but also inferences about individuals' reliability as long-term social partners.

Introduction

Whether morality demands impartiality is a longstanding debate in moral philosophy. Impartial beneficence-the view that everyone's well-being deserves equal moral consideration regardless of one's relationship to them-is regarded as a moral ideal in some ethical traditions 1, 2 . Yet other theorists argue that prioritizing the well-being of friends and family is a fundamental feature of social relationships 3, 4 . This tension raises a central question: how do people judge impartial individuals who neglect to privilege their social ties? Impartial actions may often convey conflicting moral signals, reflecting moral virtues such as fairness 5 and empathic concern 6 , while simultaneously violating relational expectations 7 . The present research examines how people evaluate the moral character of impartial and partial actors across relational contexts. We propose that, despite the appeal of impartiality, people exhibit a moral preference for partiality such that they view individuals who prioritize the wellbeing of socially close others as morally superior to those who behave impartially.

Person-centered theories of moral judgment place character assessment at the heart of moral evaluation 8, 9 , viewing moral judgments as less about actions and more about what these actions reveal about a person's underlying character. People use others' choices not only to infer what kind of person they are, but also how they are likely to behave in the future 10 . From this perspective, impartial helping (e.g., helping a stranger instead of a close other) may support two inferences about the helper, each with distinct implications for moral evaluation. On the one hand, helping a stranger provides strong evidence of a good moral character as it is less readily explained by situational pressures or self-interest 11 . Consistent with this view, prosocial actions are judged less favorably when they appear to benefit the helper 10, 12 . On the other hand, impartial helping may violate social expectations and signal a lack of loyalty. Relationship-based theories of morality propose that moral evaluations reflect a psychological adaptation that evolved to facilitate cooperation and maintain social relationships 7, 13, 14 , such that failing to prioritize close others should be seen as a moral violation.

Recent research suggests that individuals possess a moral preference for partiality. People perceive impartial actors electing to help strangers as less moral than partial actors prioritizing the well-being of close others (e.g., family members) [15] [16] [17] [18] . Relatedly, impartial actors are trusted less and judged as worse cooperation partners, although these judgments do not reliably translate into reduced cooperation during economic games 18, 19 . Yet, the inferences underlying this moral preference and its robustness across relational contexts remain less clear. One reason people may morally prefer partial actors is that they perceive social relationships as carrying special obligations 7, 13 , obligations that are violated by individuals who fail to prioritize close social ties.

The strength of these obligations, and the moral condemnation that follows from violating them, may scale with the degree of social closeness between individuals. For instance, McManus and colleagues 16 show that people perceive a greater obligation to help close (e.g., siblings) compared to more distant (e.g., cousins) relatives and that perceived obligations are associated with moral evaluations. Thus, impartial actors may be viewed as less moral to the extent that their actions violate relational obligations, with the strength of these obligations, and consequently the seriousness of their violation, scaling with social closeness.

Accurately assessing others' character is important for social well-being, allowing people to anticipate others' future behavior and avoid untrustworthy individuals who may cause them harm. Recent research suggests that people hold a moral preference for more predictable actors, with perceptions of predictability being positively associated with judgments of moral character 20, 21 . Thus, in contexts where people expect individuals to prioritize close others, impartial actors may be viewed as less moral because their actions signal unpredictability, with their failure to prioritize close others making their moral beliefs and future behavior difficult to discern. Furthermore, negative evaluations of impartial actors may be stronger for closer social ties as neglecting to prioritize especially close others may violate people's expectations to a greater extent, thereby providing a stronger signal of an unreliable moral character.

Even if implicitly, the anticipated reputational consequences of different actions play a role in motivating behavior, as suggested by research showing that people more frequently behave in ways that signal their moral quality when others are watching 22, 23 . As such, the inferences described above may not only shape how people judge partial and impartial actors but also the extent to which they prioritize the well-being of close social ties. Prior research demonstrates that people direct more help, resources, and altruistic effort toward socially close others than strangers 24, 25 . If people internalize negative evaluations of impartial actors, they should elect to behave in a more partial manner when their behavior is observable to others. By doing so, they may not only avoid damaging their social relationships but also be judged more favorably by third-party observers.

The Present Research

The present research investigates how people evaluate the moral character of partial and impartial actors across distinct moral and relational contexts. Consistent with prior work [15] [16] [17] [18] [19] , we hypothesize that actors prioritizing a socially close other over a stranger will be judged as more moral and trustworthy. We test this hypothesis using both classic sacrificial dilemmas (Experiment 1) and more ecologically valid helping scenarios (Experiments 2 and 3) as well as across relational contexts varying in genetic relatedness (i.e., kin vs. non-kin) and social closeness (e.g., friend vs. community member). Notably, we also examine when and why impartial actors are judged negatively. We propose that impartiality is evaluated unfavorably to the extent that it violates relational obligations and social expectations. Accordingly, Experiments 1-3 test whether impartial actors are perceived as less predictable than partial actors and the extent to which these perceptions of predictability are associated with moral evaluations. Similarly, Experiments 2 and 3 examine the extent to which impartial actors are viewed as violating relational obligations and whether these perceived violations predict judgments of moral character. As such, we predict that participants will exhibit a stronger preference for partiality for closer social ties on account that failing to prioritize a close other should be perceived as a greater violation of relational obligations and a stronger signal of unpredictability.

Finally, Experiment 4 examines whether a moral preference for partiality leads people to behave in a more partial manner when their actions are observable to others. Participants reported whether they would prefer to help a socially connected other (i.e., a friend, family member, or community member) in need or a stranger in greater need. We hypothesize that participants will generally prefer helping a socially connected other and that this preference will increase with social closeness. Critically, we predict that participants will behave more partially when their decision is observable to others, consistent with the possibility that people anticipate and seek to avoid negative moral evaluations associated with impartiality.

Experiment 1

Method

Participants

Eight hundred participants were recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk and received $0.50 USD upon completion of a 4-minute questionnaire. Participants were required to be residents of the United States, possess a Mechanical Turk submission approval rating of at least 95%, and pass a CAPTCHA-based verification item. We excluded participants who reported responding randomly at some point during the experiment or failed to correctly respond to two comprehension check items. These exclusion criteria helped promote data quality by removing automated and inattentive responders. The final sample was comprised of 564 participants (47% female; Mage = 39.27, SDage = 12.73). Sensitivity power analyses conducted using G*Power 26 indicated that the retained sample afforded 80% power to detect effects of approximately ηp² = .014 or larger in mixed-model analyses.

Materials and Measures

Participants were presented with two vignettes, each of which described a scenario in which an actor had the choice of sacrificing a single individual to save the lives of five others.

Both vignettes featured a friend of this actor, either as the single individual who could be sacrificed or among the five individuals who could be saved. Below each vignette was a statement describing whether the actor decided to sacrifice the single individual (Utilitarian Action) or let harm befall five individuals (Deontological Action). Consequently, this description also revealed whether the actor elected to save their friend (Partial Action) or one or more strangers (Impartial Action). Following each vignette, participants evaluated the actor across various moral dimensions presented in a randomized order within a matrix table. i Moral Perception. Participants evaluated each actor's morality and overall goodness using 7-point scales that ranged from immoral to moral and bad to good, respectively. The two judgments were strongly correlated (Partial Action: r = .87; Impartial Action: r = .89) and were i For the purposes of brevity, secondary measures (empathy, violence, intentionality, and harm) are described and analyzed in the supplementary materials (Parts A and C). averaged to create a moral perception composite, with higher values reflecting stronger perceptions of moral goodness.

Trustworthiness. Participants judged the trustworthiness of each actor using a 7-point scale that ranged from untrustworthy to trustworthy.

Predictability. Participants judged the predictability of each actor using a 7-point scale that ranged from unpredictable to predictable.

Design and Procedure

Participants were randomly assigned to either a Deontological or Utilitarian condition. In the Deontological condition, participants read two vignettes describing a hypothetical actor who chose not to sacrifice one individual to save five others. One vignette described the single individual as a friend of the actor (Partial Action), whereas the other described the single individual as a stranger and included the actor's friend among the five individuals who could be saved (Impartial Action). In contrast, participants in the Utilitarian condition were described a hypothetical actor who chose to sacrifice a single individual to save five others. Again, one vignette described the single individual as a friend of the actor (Impartial Action) while another described this individual as a stranger and placed the actor's friend among the five people who could be saved (Partial Action). Accordingly, Experiment 1 featured a 2 (Act Type: Deontological vs. Utilitarian; between-subjects) by 2 (Partiality: Partial vs. Impartial Action; within-subjects) mixed design. The presentation order of partial and impartial vignettes was counterbalanced across participants. After each vignette, participants evaluated the described actor across various moral dimensions. Next, they responded to a comprehension check question assessing their understanding of the vignette. Finally, they concluded Experiment 1 by responding to two demographic questions and a single-item measure of attentiveness.

Transparency and Openness

For all experiments, we collected our full sample prior to data analyses and report all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures used. All measures and materials presented in the current study can be viewed in the supplementary materials (Part A). Data, analyses scripts and Qualtrics survey files pertaining to each experiment are available on Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/dhybf/overview?view_only=7266bb4f6d344e619bbdd57a8bf1e294). The hypotheses, methods, and analysis plan for Experiments 2 and 3 were preregistered through Open Science Framework. These pre-registrations can be viewed via the following links (Exp 2: https://osf.io/9m26b/overview?view_only=625cdf118d3f474ea68206a6a9a15530; Exp 3: https://osf.io/fnums/overview?view_only=37a071634af1459a8a52bb4f39f685f7). We describe minor deviations from these pre-registrations in the supplementary materials (Part B).

Experiments 1 and 4 were conducted without pre-registration.

Results and Discussion

First, we examined whether participants exhibited a moral preference for partiality by evaluating actors who chose to save a close friend more favorably than those who behaved impartially. A 2 (Act Type: Deontological vs. Utilitarian) by 2 (Partiality: Partial vs. Impartial Action) mixed ANOVA on moral perceptions revealed a main effect of Partiality, F(1, 562) = 8.36, p = .004, ηp² = .015, such that partial actors were viewed as more moral (M = 4.32, SD = 1.70) than impartial actors (M = 4.20, SD = 1.78). This effect did not differ across act types, as indicated by the absence of a Partiality by Act Type interaction (p = .823). Nevertheless, we did observe a main effect of Act Type, F(1, 562) = 221.68, p < .001, ηp² = .283. Consistent with prior work 20, 27 , deontological actors were judged as more moral (M = 5.24, SD = 1.28) than utilitarian actors (M = 3.46, SD = 1.51). The same pattern emerged for judgments of trustworthiness.

Participants evaluated partial actors as more trustworthy than impartial actors, F(1, 562) = 77.54, p < .001, ηp² = .121, and deontological actors as more trustworthy than utilitarian actors, F(1, 562) = 314.75, p < .001, ηp² = .359. Again, the Partiality by Act Type interaction was not significant (p = .126). Therefore, actors who prioritized the well-being of a close friend were viewed more positively than those behaving impartially, regardless of whether they acted in a deontological or utilitarian manner.

Perceptions of Predictability Shape Moral Evaluations

Prior work reveals that more predictable individuals are viewed as more moral and as more desirable cooperation partners, even when their behavior involves causing additional harm 20, 21 . Thus, we examined whether partial actors were perceived as more predictable than impartial actors, and whether predictability judgments were associated with moral judgments. A 2 x 2 mixed ANOVA on predictability judgments revealed a main effect of Partiality, F(1, 562) = 143.00, p < .001, ηp² = .203, such that partial actors were perceived as more predictable (M = 4.39, SD = 1.70) than impartial actors (M = 3.71, SD = 1.71). We also observed a main effect of Act Type, F(1, 562) = 177.26, p < .001, ηp² = .240, with deontological actors perceived as more predictable (M = 4.90, SD = 1.23) than utilitarian actors (M = 3.36, SD = 1.47). The interaction between Partiality and Act Type was not significant (p = .147).

Next, we examined whether predictability judgments were associated with evaluations of morality and trustworthiness using linear mixed-effects models (Table 1). Predictability was decomposed into within-subject and between-subject components to distinguish participants' general tendency to perceive actors as more or less predictable from actor-specific deviations in predictability judgments. For moral evaluations, both between-subject and within-subject predictability were positively associated with perceptions of morality (Table 1; Figure 1).

Participants who generally viewed actors as more predictable also tended to view them as more moral, and, within participants, actors judged as more predictable were also judged as more moral. Act Type remained a significant predictor of moral perceptions when predictability was included in the model, whereas Partiality no longer uniquely predicted moral judgments. A similar pattern emerged for judgments of trustworthiness (Table 1), although Partiality remained a significant predictor after accounting for perceptions of predictability. In both cases, models including predictability fit the data better than models excluding it (Moral Perceptions: χ 2 (5) = 198.34, p < .001; Trustworthiness: χ 2 (5) = 252.02, p < .001). Together, these findings suggest that perceptions of predictability play an important role in shaping positive evaluations of partial actors.

Experiment 2

Although sacrificial dilemmas are useful for examining moral preferences, they depict extreme situations with low ecological validity 28 . Accordingly, in Experiment 2, we examined participants' moral evaluations of partial and impartial actors in more everyday helping contexts, in which actors chose whether to help a friend or a stranger. Consistent with relationship-based theories of moral judgment 7, 13, 14 , we predicted that participants would again exhibit a moral preference for partiality, evaluating actors who chose to help a friend as more moral and trustworthy than those who instead helped a stranger. Additionally, we examined whether partial actors would be perceived as more predictable and as better fulfilling their relational obligations, and whether these perceptions might help explain positive evaluations of partial actors.

Method

Participants

A sample of 810 U.S. residents was recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk using the same eligibility criteria as Experiment 1. Participants received $0.50 USD for completing a 4minute questionnaire. Consistent with preregistered exclusion criteria, we excluded participants who self-reported engaging in inattentive responding or failed to correctly respond to two comprehension check questions. Our final sample comprised of 497 participants (42% female; Mage = 40.73, SDage = 13.36). Sensitivity power analyses indicated that this sample provided 80% power to detect effects of d = 0.12 or larger in the preregistered paired-samples t-tests.

Materials and Measures

Experiment 2 featured two vignettes adapted from McManus and colleagues 15 . These vignettes described a situation in which both a hypothetical actor's close friend and a stranger were in need of assistance. Each vignette was followed by a brief statement describing whether the actor decided to help their friend (Partial Action) or the stranger (Impartial Action). As in Experiment 1, participants evaluated each actor on several moral dimensions. Judgments of moral goodness (i.e., moral perceptions), trustworthiness, and predictability were assessed using the same measures as in Experiment 1. Inspired by relationship-based theories of moral judgment 7, 14 , participants also evaluated the extent to which each actor fulfilled their social obligations.

Social Obligation.

Participants judged the extent to which each actor fulfilled their social obligations using a 7-point scale that ranged from completely violated obligations to completely fulfilled obligations.

Design and Procedure

Experiment 2 employed a fully within-subjects design. Participants viewed two vignettes: one in which a hypothetical actor helped a friend rather than a stranger (Partial Action), and one in which an actor helped a stranger rather than a friend (Impartial Action).

The presentation order of vignettes was counterbalanced across participants. After each vignette, participants evaluated the actor across several moral dimensions and completed a comprehension check item assessing their understanding of the scenario. Participants then responded to two demographic items and a single-item measure of attentiveness before concluding the experiment.

Results and Discussion

Consistent with Experiment 1, partial actors were judged as more moral, t(496) = 13.82, p < .001, d = 0.62, 95% CI [0.52, 0.72], and more trustworthy, t(496) = 20.67, p < .001, d = 0.93, 95% CI [0.82, 1.03], than impartial actors. Partial actors were also perceived as more predictable, t(496) = 32.23, p < .001, d = 1.45, 95% CI [1.32, 1.57], and as better fulfilling their social obligations, t(496) = 17.10, p < .001, d = 0.77, 95% CI [0.67, 0.87]. Thus, we again observed a moral preference for partiality, this time within a more ecologically valid helping context. Actors who prioritized the well-being of a friend were viewed as more moral, trustworthy, and predictable, while also being perceived as better fulfilling their relational obligations.

Perceptions of Predictability and Social Obligation Shape Moral Evaluations

Next, we examined whether judgments of predictability and social obligation were associated with moral evaluations. As in Experiment 1, predictability judgments were decomposed into within-subject and between-subject components. The same decomposition was applied to judgments of social obligation. Both within-subject and between-subject variation in perceived predictability and social obligation were positively associated with moral perceptions (Table 2). Participants who generally perceived actors as more predictable and as better fulfilling their social obligations also tended to view them as more moral. Likewise, within participants, actors perceived as more predictable and as better fulfilling their social obligations were also judged as more moral. Importantly, Partiality no longer predicted moral evaluations after accounting for predictability and social obligation judgments. We also observed a Partiality by Predictability interaction (Table 2; Figure 2), such that predictability was positively associated with moral evaluations for partial actors, b = 0.23, 95% CI [0.14, 0.31], t(930) = 5.00, p < .001, but was not reliably associated with evaluations of impartial actors, b = -0.07, 95% CI [-0.16, 0.01], t(930) = -1.65, p = .099. Model comparisons indicated that including predictability and social obligation judgments substantially improved model fit relative to models excluding one or both predictors (all χ 2 > 33.53, all p < .001).

Experiment 3

Experiments 1 and 2 revealed a moral preference for actors who prioritized close others over strangers. In Experiment 3, we examined whether this preference varies across different social relationships. People are generally more willing to help family members than friends, and friends than strangers 24, 29 and perceive stronger obligations toward closer ties 7, 16 . Accordingly, we manipulated whether the known individual in need of assistance was a family member, friend, or community member to examine whether participants' preference for partiality varies across relational contexts, and, importantly, whether perceptions of predictability and social obligation help explain moral evaluations of partial and impartial actors across these contexts.

Participants

A sample of 1204 U.S residents was recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk using the same eligibility criteria as Experiments 1 and 2. Participants received $0.50 USD after completing a 4-minute questionnaire. Consistent with preregistered exclusion criteria, we excluded participants who self-reported inattentive responding or failed to correctly respond to comprehension check items. Following exclusions, we retained a sample of 901 participants (52% female; Mage = 39.25, SDage = 13.66). Sensitivity power analyses indicated that this sample provided 80% power to detect effects of approximately ηp² = .011 or larger for the preregistered mixed-model analyses.

Measures and Materials

Experiment 3 featured three vignettes, two of which were identical to those used in Experiment 2. Each vignette described a situation in which both a stranger and a known individual required help. Depending on condition, the known individual was described as a close friend, relative, or member of the same community as a hypothetical actor able to provide help.

Following each vignette, participants read a brief statement indicating whether the actor chose to help the known individual (Partial Action), the stranger (Impartial Action), or neither individual (No Help Action). Participants then evaluated each actor on the same moral dimensions assessed in Experiment 2.

Design and Procedure

Experiment 3 featured a 3 (Relationship: Friend, Relative, Community Member; between-subjects) by 3 (Partiality: Partial Action, Impartial Action, No Help Action; withinsubjects) mixed design. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three Relationship conditions, which determined the relationship between the known individual and the hypothetical actor in each vignette. Regardless of condition, participants viewed three vignettes: one in which the actor helped the known individual, one in which they helped the stranger, and one in which they chose not to help either individual. The pairing of actions with vignettes, and the presentation order of the resulting items, was counterbalanced, such that each combination and order was equally likely to occur. Because the present research focuses on moral evaluations of partial versus impartial actions, judgments of actors who chose not to help either individual were not analyzed here, as these actors differed not in whom they helped, but in whether they helped at all. ii Following each vignette, participants judged the actor on various moral dimensions and responded to a comprehension check question. Participants then completed three items assessing their beliefs about the morality of helping family, friends, and community members before strangers, followed by two demographic questions and a single-item measure of attentiveness.

ii Not surprisingly, actors who chose not to help either individual were judged as less moral and trustworthy than both partial and impartial actors (all p < .001, all d > 0.62).

Results and Discussion

We conducted a 3 (Relationship: Friend, Relative, Community Member) by 2 (Partiality: Partial Action, Impartial Action) mixed ANOVA to test whether partial actors were perceived as more moral than impartial actors and whether the magnitude of this effect varied across relationship contexts. This analysis revealed a main effect of Partiality, F(1, 898) = 330.49, p < .001, ηp² = .269. As hypothesized, partial actors were judged as more moral (M = 5.65, SD = 1.09) than impartial actors (M = 4.70, SD = 1.38). We also observed a Partiality by Relationship interaction, F(2, 898) = 10.79, p < .001, ηp² = .023 (Figure 3). Follow-up contrasts indicated that the moral preference for partiality was stronger for family members compared to friends, b = 0.26, 95% CI [0.01, 0.51], t(898) = 2.06, p = .040, d = 0.14, and stronger for friends compared to community members, b = 0.33, 95% CI [0.08, 0.58], t(898) = 2.59, p = .010, d = 0.17. iii A similar pattern emerged for judgments of trustworthiness. There was a main effect of Partiality, F(1, 898) = 629.45, p < .001, ηp² = .412, as well as a Partiality by Relationship interaction, F(2, 898) = 6.96, p = .001, ηp² = .015. Follow-up contrasts revealed that this interaction was driven by a weaker partiality effect in the Community Member condition relative to both the Friend, b = 0.47, 95% CI [0.20, 0.75], t(898) = 3.40, p < .001, d = 0.23, and Relative, b = 0.43, 95% CI [0.15, 0.70], t(898) = 3.07, p = .002, d = 0.20, conditions. Conversely, the effect of partiality on judgments of trust did not differ between Friend and Relative conditions (p = .734). Thus, these findings suggest that relational closeness amplifies individuals' moral preference for partiality.

iii Moral evaluations of partial and impartial actors were consistent with participants' explicit beliefs about the morality of prioritizing close others over strangers (Supplementary Materials Part C). Next, we examined whether partial actors were again perceived as more predictable and as better fulfilling their social obligations, and whether the magnitude of these effects varied across relationship contexts. Analyses of predictability judgments revealed a main effect of Partiality, F(1, 898) = 2233.91, p < .001, ηp² = .713, as well as a significant Partiality by Relationship interaction, F(2, 898) = 10.66, p < .001, ηp² = .023. Consistent with Experiments 1 and 2, partial actors were perceived as more predictable (M = 5.65, SD = 1.19) than impartial actors (M = 2.57, SD = 1.33). Follow-up contrasts indicated that this effect was weaker in the Community Member condition compared to both the Friend, b = 0.65, 95% CI [0.34, 0.97], t(898) = 4.07, p < .001, d = 0.27, and Relative, b = 0.63, 95% CI [0.32, 0.95], t(898) = 3.96, p < .001, d = 0.26, conditions, which themselves did not differ (p = .899). The same pattern emerged for judgments of social obligation. There was a main effect of Partiality, F(1, 898) = 508.82, p < .001, ηp² = .362, such that partial actors were judged as better fulfilling their social obligations (M = 5.42, SD = 1.31) relative to impartial actors (M = 4.04, SD = 1.43). We also observed a significant Partiality by Relationship interaction, F(2, 898) = 16.81, p < .001, ηp² = .036, again driven by a weaker partiality effect in the Community Member condition relative to both the Friend, b = 0.62, 95% CI [0.33, 0.91], t(898) = 4.15, p < .001, d = 0.28, and Relative, b = 0.84, 95% CI [0.54, 1.13], t(898) = 5.61, p < .001, d = 0.37 conditions. Thus, partial actors were again viewed as more predictable and as fulfilling more of their social obligations than impartial actors, particularly when prioritizing socially close-relative to more distant-social ties.

Perceptions of Predictability and Social Obligation Shape Moral Evaluations

Finally, we examined whether judgments of predictability and social obligation were associated with moral evaluations using linear mixed-effects models. As in Experiment 2, predictability and social obligation judgments were decomposed into within-subject and between-subject components. Replicating the results of Experiment 2, both within-subject and between-subject variation in these judgments were positively associated with perceptions of moral goodness (Table 3). That is, perceiving actors, in general, as more predictable and as fulfilling more of their social obligations was associated with judging them as more moral.

Similarly, within participants, actors viewed as more predictable and as better fulfilling their social obligations were also viewed as more moral. Notably, Partiality was no longer a reliable predictor of moral evaluations after accounting for predictability and social obligation judgments (Table 3).

Predictability judgments were positively associated with moral evaluations of partial, b = 0.22, 95% CI [0.15, 0.29], t(1711) = 6.33, p < .001, but not impartial actors, b = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.09, 0.04], t(1711) = -0.70, p = .487. Furthermore, while social obligation judgments were positively associated with evaluations of both partial, b = 0.40, 95% CI [0.32, 0.47], t(1714) = 10.75, p < .001, and impartial actors, b = 0.61, 95% CI [0.54, 0.68], t(1714) = 16.57, p < .001, this association was stronger for impartial actors. Neither predictability nor social obligation judgments interacted with Relationship to predict moral evaluations (all p > .106), suggesting that these associations emerged consistently across relationships varying in social closeness. iv Model comparisons indicated that including predictability and social obligation judgments significantly improved model fit relative to models excluding one or both of these judgments (all χ 2 > 64.05, all p < .001). The same pattern of results emerged for judgments of trustworthiness (Table 3). Taken together, these findings suggest that, across relationship contexts, individuals' moral preference for partiality is closely tied to their perceptions of actors' predictability and fulfillment of social obligations. iv Accordingly, relationship-related terms were omitted from the models reported in Table 3.

Experiment 4

Experiments 1-3 demonstrated that people view individuals who prioritize close others over strangers as more moral and trustworthy. Experiment 4 examined whether this moral preference is reflected in individuals' own helping decisions. Participants chose whether to help a socially close other or a stranger in greater need, allowing us to assess whether people themselves prioritize close others in everyday helping contexts. We also examined whether anonymity moderates these decisions. If people have internalized social norms favoring partiality, they should be more likely to prioritize close others when their behavior is publicly observable, given that failing to do so may not only risk damaging an important relationship but lead to negative moral evaluations from observers. Accordingly, we predicted that participants would be more likely to behave partially when their choices were public rather than private.

Participants

Six hundred and three U.S. residents were recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk using the same eligibility criteria as Experiments 1-3. Participants received $0.50 USD upon completing a 4-minute questionnaire. We excluded data from 212 participants who self-reported inattentive responding or failed to correctly respond to comprehension check questions. The final sample consisted of 391 participants (53% female; Mage = 39.55, SDage = 13.45). Sensitivity power analyses indicated that this sample afforded 80% power to detect effects of ηp² = .024 or larger for the assessed between-subjects interaction.

Measures and Materials

Participants were presented with a vignette describing a situation in which two individuals were seeking financial assistance online to help repair flood damage to their homes following a severe storm. Within the vignette, participants read about a hypothetical actor ("Michael") who had decided to donate $100 to one of these individuals. One individual was described as socially connected to Michael-either his friend, relative, or a member of his community, depending on Relationship condition-whereas the other individual was described as a stranger. Participants were asked which individual they would donate to if they were in Michael's position: the known individual or the stranger. They then responded to the question, "How difficult would this decision be for you?" using a 7-point scale that ranged from 1 (Not at all difficult) to 7 (Extremely difficult). Next, participants were informed that the stranger's home had been damaged more severely and would require significantly more money to repair (i.e., compared to the home of Michael's friend, relative, or community member). Participants again indicated which individual they would donate to and rated how difficult this decision would be using the same 7-point scale. Thus, the second donation decision assessed whether participants would prioritize a socially close other even when a stranger was in greater need.

Design and Procedure

Experiment 4 featured a 3 (Relationship: Friend, Relative, Community Member) by 2 (Donation Anonymity: Public, Private) between-subjects design. Participants randomly assigned to the Public condition were instructed to imagine that their donation decision would be publicly visible online. Conversely, those assigned to the Private condition were told that their decision would remain completely anonymous. Following the donation task, participants responded to a comprehension check question and exploratory measures assessing whether they prioritize being helpful or appearing helpful (Supplementary Materials Part A). They concluded Experiment 4 by responding to two demographic questions and a single-item measure of attentiveness.

Results and Discussion

Participants exhibited a strong preference for partiality in their donation decisions. When a known individual and a stranger were described as being in equal need, a large majority of participants (97%) elected to donate to the known individual, χ 2 (1) = 340.73, p < .001. Even after learning that the stranger was in greater need, a smaller-but still clear-majority of participants (66%) continued to prioritize the known individual, χ 2 (1) = 42.56, p < .001 (Figure 5). We used binary logistic regressions to examine whether Relationship (Friend, Relative, Community Member), Donation Anonymity (Public, Private), and their interaction predicted participants' donation decisions. We focused on participants' second donation choice-made after learning that the stranger was in greater need-because participants overwhelmingly chose to donate to the known individual prior to this information, regardless of condition. Analyses of participants' second donation choice revealed a main effect of Relationship, χ 2 (2) = 13.79, p = .001.

Participants were more likely to donate to the known individual rather than the stranger in greater need when the known individual was a friend, OR = 2.62, 95% CI [1.38, 4.96], z = 3.53, p = .001, or relative, OR = 1.95, 95% CI [1.04, 3.63], z = 2.50, p = .033, compared with a community member. Thus, preferences for partiality were stronger in the case of close, rather than more distant, social ties. v We also observed a main effect of Donation Anonymity, χ 2 (1) = 11.00, p < .001. Participants were more likely to donate to the stranger in greater need when their donation decision was private rather than publicly observable, OR = 2.09, 95% CI [1.34, 3.25], z = 3.28, p = .001. Thus, observability increased participants' tendency to prioritize socially close others, suggesting that participants may have been aware of and considered the reputational consequences of impartiality.

v Participants' donation decisions were again consistent with their explicit beliefs about the morality of prioritizing close others over strangers (Supplementary Materials Part C). We next examined judgments of decision difficulty using a 3 x 2 between-subjects ANOVA. This analysis revealed a main effect of Relationship, F(2, 385) = 3.03, p = .049, ηp² = .016, such that participants reported greater difficulty deciding whom to help when the known individual was more socially distant. In contrast, Donation Anonymity did not influence decision difficulty, F(1, 385) = 0.46, p = .500, ηp² = .001. Thus, although anonymity altered participants' donation choices, it did not appear to change the subjective difficulty of the moral conflict itself.

We did not observe a Relationship by Donation Anonymity interaction for either donation decisions, χ 2 (2) = 0.23, p = .893, or judgments of decision difficulty, F(2, 385) = 0.27, p = .761, ηp² = .001. Taken together, these findings suggest that individuals exhibit a robust behavioral preference for partiality, even when a stranger is objectively in greater need of help. Moreover, this preference was sensitive to social observability: participants were more willing to behave impartially when their decisions were anonymous, consistent with the possibility that publicly observable helping decisions are shaped, in part, by the anticipated social costs of impartiality.

General Discussion

Participants demonstrated a consistent moral preference for partiality. Actors who prioritized socially close others over strangers were judged as more moral and trustworthy across both classic sacrificial dilemmas and more ecologically valid helping contexts. Thus, despite impartial beneficence being a central tenet of many moral philosophies 1,2 , everyday moral judgments appear to favor those who prioritize close others. The present research provides insight into why impartial actors are viewed less favorably. Across experiments, impartial actors were perceived as less predictable and as fulfilling less of their social obligations, with these perceptions being associated with less favorable moral evaluations. Thus, moral evaluations of impartial actors may not simply reflect the perceived morality of their actions, but assessments of what these actions reveal about their reliability as long-term cooperation partners.

Moral judgments have been theorized to serve as a psychological adaptation that facilitates cooperation 7, 13, 14 . Accordingly, individuals who defy social expectations or violate relational obligations, even when helping strangers, may be viewed as immoral or untrustworthy because their actions signal poor relational reliability. That is, failing to prioritize close others may signal than an individual is unlikely to honor the obligations associated with close relationships. Similarly, impartial actions, when defying social expectations, may make a person's motives and future behavior more difficult to discern, generating social uncertainty and undermining trust 20, 21, 30 . Although the present research cannot establish the precise causal role of these perceptions, the robust associations observed across paradigms suggest that perceived unpredictability and relational violations contribute to the reputational costs of impartiality.

The present findings also highlight the importance of relational context in moral judgment. Although moral psychology has traditionally ignored the role of social relationships 28 , recent work has begun to examine how relationships shape moral evaluations [15] [16] [17] [18] [19] 31 . Building on this work, the present findings demonstrate that the moral preference for partiality varies across relational contexts. Actors who failed to prioritize a family member or friend were judged more negatively than those who failed to prioritize a member of their community. Judgments of predictability and social obligation were similarly influenced by relational context: impartial actors were viewed as less predictable and as violating their social obligations to a greater extent when they failed to help socially close rather than more distant others. Thus, the reputational costs of impartiality depend, in part, on the closeness of the relationship being neglected.

A preference for partiality also emerged in participants' own helping decisions. In Experiment 4, most participants preferred to help a socially connected other over a stranger, even when the stranger was in greater need. This preference was particularly pronounced when the familiar other was a close social tie (e.g., friend). Notably, participants were more likely to choose the impartial option when their decision was described as anonymous rather than publicly observable. This finding suggests that helping decision are shaped by reputational concerns, with publicly failing to help a close social tie risking not only relational strain with the neglected individual but moral condemnation from observers.

These findings extend prior research showing that prosocial behavior increases under observation 22, 32, 33 by suggesting that observation shapes not only whether people behave generously, but also whom they choose to help. More broadly, they highlight a potential tension between impartial moral ideals and the relational expectations that shape everyday moral behavior. People may regard impartiality as morally admirable in principle while nevertheless anticipating negative social consequences for acting impartially in contexts where close others are expected to receive priority. This tension may be particularly relevant for effective altruism movements, which encourage adherents not only to endorse impartiality as a moral ideal but also to act on it publicly. The present findings suggest that, at least in some interpersonal contexts, impartial helping carries reputational costs, particularly when it involves neglecting close social ties. Consequently, promoting impartial giving may require not only appealing to aggregate welfare and fairness, but also addressing the relational expectations that shape everyday moral evaluations.

Limitations and Future Directions

The present work is not without limitations. First, the present findings were observed in a sample of U.S. residents recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk, raising questions about the generalizability of these effects across populations. Although prior work suggests that perceptions of relational obligations and preferences for predictable social partners are widespread 14, 20 cultural variation likely exists in the extent to which partiality is morally valued.

Future research should seek to examine these effects in non-WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic) populations, including within cultures that place differing emphasis on collectivism and kinship obligations.

Second, the present research relied on hypothetical vignettes and self-reported donation preferences. Although such methods are common in moral psychology, they necessarily simplify the complexity of moral decisions in real interpersonal contexts. Future research could examine whether similar patterns emerge in behavioral paradigms involving real financial stakes or repeated cooperation. For example, it would be informative to assess whether people preferentially cooperate with impartial actors in interactive economic games, and whether such behavior is mediated by perceptions of predictability or relational obligations. Similarly, future work may examine whether real-world donation decisions exhibit a preference for partiality and whether this preference is mitigated by anonymity.

Conclusion

Across four experiments, people consistently preferred actors who prioritized close others over strangers. Partial actors were viewed as more predictable and as better fulfilling their social obligations than impartial actors, and these perceptions were associated with more favorable judgments of their moral character. Participants' own prosocial preferences also exhibited partiality, with most electing to help a socially connected other even when a stranger was in greater need. Despite the moral appeal of impartiality 1, 2, 6 , the present findings suggest that everyday moral judgments are deeply shaped by relational obligations and concerns about social reliability. Thus, moral evaluations may be guided less by detached assessments of whether actions conform to abstract moral principles and more by pragmatic inferences about what those actions reveal about a person's value as a long-term cooperation partner.

Similarly, perceived fulfillment of social obligations was positively associated with trust for both partial, b = 0.41, 95% CI [0.31, 0.51], t(985) = 8.17, p < .001, and impartial actors, b = 0.63, 95% CI [0.53, 0.73], t(985) = 12.62, p < .001, although the association was stronger for impartial actors. Model comparisons again indicated that models including predictability and social obligation judgments fit the data better than models excluding these predictors (all χ 2 > 77.33, all p < .001). Together, these findings suggest that perceptions of predictability and relational obligation play an important role in shaping positive evaluations of partial actors in everyday helping contexts.
